quote: "The greatest flaw in life is that it is always imperfect, and that a certain part of it is postponed. One who daily puts the finishing touches to his life is never in want of time." — Seneca, Letters to Lucilius 101
context:
Seneca wrote this letter to answer a specific piece of news. A capable Roman knight named Cornelius Senecio, a man Lucilius knew, had climbed from humble beginnings toward real fortune; the hard part of his life was behind him and the road ahead looked downhill. Then he died, suddenly, with his plans still open on the table. Seneca's point is not that death is near, a thing everyone already knows. It is that a life which leaves its meaning deferred to some later date is the life most exposed to bad timing. The man who completes himself daily cannot be caught short.

This week the British novelist Jeffrey Archer died at 86, one day before the scheduled publication of Adam & Eve, the book he had already decided would be his last. He finished the work. He did not live to see it in a reader's hands. The two things, it turns out, were never the same event. Senecio's lesson holds: the part of your effort you control is the doing of it, which you can complete, not the reception of it, which arrives on its own schedule or not at all.
question: If no one ever saw the result, would the work you are postponing still be worth finishing today?
